title: Freedom and Collapse
content_html:
Freedom and Collapse

Agency is influenced indeterminacy.

We do not control randomness; we cultivate conditions under which meaning‑compatible outcomes become likely. Freedom lives where uncertainty meets commitment.

Freedom and Collapse

The language of quantum theory offers a tempting metaphor for choice: before a decision, many possibilities coexist; after, one outcome is actual. But indeterminacy by itself does not deliver freedom—pure randomness is not agency. Equally, strict determinism would erase agency. The middle path is emergent agency: a self‑organising system that shapes how uncertainty resolves without commanding it from outside the causal weave.

In a living brain, noisy dynamics and probabilistic synaptic updates supply variation; learned models, goals, and attention supply constraints. Freedom becomes influenced indeterminacy— the skill of biasing probability distributions in service of values and predictions. We do not choose outcomes ex nihilo; rather, we curate the conditions under which some outcomes become more likely than others.

Three nested layers of “the free”

  • Physical indeterminacy — quantum and thermodynamic fluctuations provide genuine variability.
  • Neural self‑organisation — plastic circuits turn variability into adaptive exploration, settling into metastable patterns that encode skills, preferences, and habits.
  • Conscious guidance — attention and narrative integrate goals, norms, and context, gently steering the resolution of ambiguity toward lived commitments.

Freedom is not the absence of causes but the presence of self‑causes—recurrent loops in which memory, prediction, and perception co‑tune how possibilities become actual.

  • Freedom grows with model quality: better predictions widen effective options while reducing regret.
  • Freedom is trained: habits are frozen choices; practice re‑sculpts the probability landscape.
  • Freedom is relational: constraints (body, culture, ecology) are not the enemy of agency; they are its scaffolding.

Select – Change – Reconstruct

  • Select — narrowing the feasible set (shaping priors; attending to salient cues).
  • Change — updating internal models via action and feedback (plasticity; policy refinement).
  • Reconstruct — narrating the outcome into identity and meaning (integrating the choice into the ongoing story of self and world).

References

  • Dennett, D. (2003/2014). Freedom Evolves; Elbow Room.
  • Kane, R. (2005). A Contemporary Introduction to Free Will.
  • Dehaene, S. (2014). Consciousness and the Brain (decision evidence accumulation).

  • Gazzaniga, M. (2011). Who’s in Charge? (neuroscience and responsibility).
